title: Single-Minded Exclusive Recitation
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Answer: Single-minded exclusive recitation means always reciting the Buddha with one mind, with no other thoughts — that is, as Master Shandao taught, “recitation thought after thought, until the end of life.”

inline.s: Question: What is single-minded exclusive recitation?
Answer:
“Single-minded exclusive recitation” means: always reciting the Buddha with one mind, with no other thoughts.
That is, as Master Shandao taught:
“Recitation thought after thought, until the end of life.”
Master Shandao taught:
“An uninterrupted succession brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life
(if one practices thus all one’s life —
that is, one who practices single-minded exclusive recitation
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
(For details, see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
“Single-minded” (yixiang)
means “always”;
“exclusive recitation” (zhuannian)
means reciting with a focused, single-minded intent — that is, reciting the Buddha with one mind. Therefore,
single-minded exclusive recitation” means: always reciting the Buddha with one mind.
“One mind”
means the mind is single and concentrated, not scattered. In his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan
clearly taught:
“One mind” means thought following thought in succession, with no other thoughts intermingled.
(For details, see
Master Tanluan’s Pure Land Teaching
) Master Zhizhe said:
If the mind dwells in mindfulness,
thought following thought
, with no other mind interrupting
(not interrupted by other thoughts)
then it is called one mind
(Commentary on the Meaning of Avalokiteshvara)
One mind is concentrating the mind single-pointedly, with no second thought
, and it is also what Master Yongming, a reincarnation of Amitābha Buddha, called “
no other thoughts
(no thoughts other than this).” Master Yongming said:
When walking in meditation
(circumambulation)
and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha and making vows, be earnest, toilsome, and sincere,
with no other thoughts
, as though facing execution, as though locked in prison
(bi (
bì
) prison: a jail)
, pursued by enemies and bandits, pressed by water and fire,
single-mindedly

crying for rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, broadly to deliver sentient beings, to perpetuate and exalt the Three Jewels, and vowing to repay the four kindnesses. Such sincerity is surely not cast away in vain.”

(Translation: When walking in meditation and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha and making vows, be earnest and sincere, with no distracting thoughts, as though about to be executed, as though locked in prison, as though pursued by enemies and bandits, as though pressed by water and fire; urgently,
single-mindedly

crying for rescue, wishing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly to realize the unborn, broadly to deliver sentient beings, to perpetuate and exalt the Three Jewels, and vowing to repay the four kindnesses. With such sincerity, the effort is not cast away in vain, and one is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
(Collected Writings on the Ten Thousand Good Deeds Returning to One)
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu
in the Treatise on Rebirth says:
“The mind constantly makes vows,
single-mindedly
reciting exclusively
, in the end to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, wishing
truly to practice śamatha
(calming)
[Śamatha] Translated as “calming.” To calm is
to still all distracting thoughts.
Therefore,
“single-minded exclusive recitation” means: always reciting the Buddha with one mind, with no other thoughts.
This is of the utmost importance in Pure Land practice; it is the main theme of Pure Land practice. Hence Master Shandao, a reincarnation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
“An uninterrupted succession brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life
(one who practices thus all one’s life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
(For details, see
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching
In the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, the Buddha said:

The devas and people of the worlds in the ten directions who sincerely wish to be born in that land are of three grades. Those of the highest grade renounce home and desire, become śramaṇas, give rise to the mind of enlightenment, and
single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha,

cultivating various merits and wishing to be born in that land. When such beings approach the end of life, Amitāyus Buddha, together with a great assembly, appears before them, and they at once follow that Buddha and are reborn in his land, where they are naturally born by transformation from within seven-jeweled lotus flowers, abide in the state of non-retrogression, and are possessed of brave wisdom and unimpeded supernatural powers.”

Those of the middle grade are the devas and people of the worlds in the ten directions who sincerely wish to be born in that land. Though they cannot become śramaṇas and cultivate great merits, they should give rise to the supreme mind of enlightenment and
single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitāyus Buddha,

cultivating good deeds to a greater or lesser extent, observing the precepts and fasts, erecting stupas and images, giving food to śramaṇas, hanging banners and lighting lamps, scattering flowers and burning incense, and dedicating all this in order to be born in that land. At the time of death, Amitāyus Buddha manifests a transformation body, radiant and endowed with all the marks, just like the real Buddha, and together with a great assembly appears before them. They at once follow the transformation Buddha and are reborn in his land, abiding in non-retrogression, their merit and wisdom next only to those of the highest grade.”
[Give rise to the mind of enlightenment] To give rise to the great mind that seeks the Buddha path above (perfect enlightenment and Buddhahood) and delivers sentient beings below.
Single-minded Buddha-recitation is supremely excellent.
Single-minded Buddha-recitation comprises the three studies of precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Master Lianchi said:

Precepts mean preventing wrongdoing: if one can recite the Buddha single-mindedly, no evil dares enter — that is precepts. Concentration means dispelling distraction: if one recites the Buddha single-mindedly and the mind does not cling to other objects
(the mind does not grasp at other things)

, that is concentration. Wisdom means clear illumination: if one contemplates each syllable of the Buddha’s name distinctly, and also contemplates that both the reciter and the recited are unobtainable, that is wisdom. To recite the Buddha in this way is to embody precepts, concentration, and wisdom.”
(Collected Pure Land Sayings of Yunqi)
Single-minded Buddha-recitation fully encompasses the six perfections and the myriad practices
. Master Lianchi said:

“Now, when one recites the Buddha single-mindedly, the ten thousand conditions are naturally relinquished — this is the perfection of giving; when one recites the Buddha single-mindedly, all evils naturally cease — this is the perfection of morality; when one recites the Buddha single-mindedly, the mind naturally becomes gentle — this is the perfection of patience; when one recites the Buddha single-mindedly, one never retreats or falls — this is the perfection of vigor; when one recites the Buddha single-mindedly, no other thoughts arise — this is the perfection of meditative concentration; when one recites the Buddha single-mindedly, right mindfulness is clear and distinct — this is the perfection of wisdom. Extending this to the utmost, it does not go beyond the single mind, and all the myriad practices are complete.”
(Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra)
For details, see
Single-Minded Buddha-Recitation, Not Scattered-Mind Recitation
Question: Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles says:

“Although I have explained above the benefits of the two gates of meditative and non-meditative good, looking to the Buddha’s fundamental vow, the intent is that sentient beings should single-mindedly and exclusively recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.”
What does “single-mindedly and exclusively recite” mean?
Answer:

The two gates of meditative and non-meditative” refers to meditative good and non-meditative good. The thirteen contemplations from the contemplation of the sun downward are called meditative good, and the three blessed practices and nine grades are called non-meditative good. The meaning of Master Shandao’s words is this: although he has explained above the merits of meditative good and non-meditative good, looking up to the World-Honored One’s fundamental vow, the intent is in fact to have sentient beings exclusively uphold the Name in recitation.
So here, “
single-mindedly and exclusively recite”
means:
one must exclusively uphold the Name in recitation.
In the Two Practices of Pure Karma, Exclusive and Mixed, Master Shandao also specially explained this meaning. The Master taught:
“Sentient beings’ obstructions are heavy, the object is subtle and the mind coarse, consciousness is stirred and spirit flies about, so contemplation is hard to accomplish. Therefore the great sage
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
, out of compassion,
directly exhorts
the exclusive recitation of the name
Precisely because name-recitation is easy
(precisely because reciting the name is easier than contemplation)
an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth

(Translation: Sentient beings’ karmic obstructions are heavy, the object contemplated is subtle while the mind is coarse, consciousness is stirred and spirit flies about, and so contemplation of the Buddha is hard to accomplish. Therefore Śākyamuni Buddha, out of compassion, directly taught them to uphold the Name in recitation — exclusively reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha. Precisely because reciting the name is easier than contemplation, at the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues in succession, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.)
Once the general direction of Pure Land practice — exclusive name-recitation (
“exclusively recite the name, and an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth”
) — is established, the question that immediately follows is: how should one ensure
that the thought of reciting the Buddha continues in succession at the moment of death
? Therefore Master Shandao then further taught:
“If one can
continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life,
(one who practices thus all one’s life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”

[Continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life] Because at the moment of death, if the thought of reciting the Buddha continues in succession, one is reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one must practice in this way all one’s life, letting recitation thought after thought become second nature through accumulated practice. Then one is certain to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss — ten out of ten, a hundred out of a hundred. [Become second nature through accumulated practice] Through continuous, repeated practice, recitation thought after thought becomes instinctive.
Therefore, Master Shandao, a reincarnation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:
“Exclusively recite the name, and an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth.”
For this, one must
“continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life,”
letting recitation thought after thought become second nature through accumulated practice. Thus is established the guiding principle of Pure Land practice:
Exclusively recite the name, and an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth; continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life.

This thoroughly and perfectly resolves the fundamental question of Pure Land practice: which method of Buddha-recitation should be adopted, and how should one recite, so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss! These sixteen
great characters
are the golden highway to the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss
and are the essence of Master Shandao’s Pure Land teaching. One who practices thus,
ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn, forever receiving the Dharma-joy of the unconditioned, until one attains Buddhahood — is this not delightful!
From the above we can see that in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles,
the “single-mindedly and exclusively recite” and the “single-minded exclusive recitation” in the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life differ greatly in meaning;
the two must not be used interchangeably
As to how one correctly upholds the name,
the twelfth Pure Land patriarch, Master Chewu, taught:
“What is called upholding the Name is wholeheartedly embracing it in the breast
— holding it firmly in the mind without a moment’s forgetting.
If a single thought is slightly interrupted
(if the thought of reciting the Buddha is slightly interrupted by a deluded thought)
, then it is not upholding. If a single thought is slightly mixed
(if a deluded thought is slightly mixed in)
, then it is not upholding. Thought following thought without mixture or interruption — that is true vigor.
With unceasing vigor,
one gradually enters single-minded, undistracted concentration
and perfectly accomplishes the Pure Land karma.”
(The Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)
[Wholeheartedly embracing it in the breast (
yīng

)] “Wholeheartedly” (quanquan): clenching and not letting go, extended to mean earnestness. “Embracing in the breast” (fuying): remembering in the heart. “Wholeheartedly embracing it in the breast” describes earnestly remembering and never forgetting.
Question: Master Shandao said: “The Buddha teaches us to recite Amitābha with devotion upon devotion.” What does this mean?
Answer: This line comes from Master Shandao’s Verses in Praise of the Dharma Service. The Verses in Praise of the Dharma Service say:
“The Land of Bliss — nirvāṇa’s unconditioned sphere — with scattered, casual good is hard to gain. So the Tathāgata
(Śākyamuni Buddha)
chose the essential way here, teaching: recite Amitābha with devotion once again.”

“Teaching us to recite Amitābha with devotion upon devotion” means: Śākyamuni Buddha taught sentient beings to recite Amitābha Buddha with ever greater single-mindedness, again and again — that is, the work of Buddha-recitation must grow ever deeper and more refined.

“Scattered good” refers to good deeds not done in accordance with the practice of the rebirth sūtras, also called “mixed practice.” As to right practice and mixed practice (all other good deeds besides right practice), Master Shandao gave clear instruction in the Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles, and he very much emphasized that right practice must be done with
one mind
. The following is excerpted and annotated:

Now, practice is of two kinds: first, right practice; second, mixed practice. “Right practice” means practice done exclusively in accordance with the rebirth sūtras — this is called right practice. What are these?
Single-mindedly
reciting and reading exclusively this Contemplation Sūtra, the Amitābha Sūtra, the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, and so on;
single-mindedly
contemplating, observing, and recollecting the adornments of the two kinds of reward in that land. If one bows, then
single-mindedly
bow exclusively to that Buddha; if one recites with the mouth, then
single-mindedly
recite exclusively that Buddha’s name; if one praises and makes offerings, then
single-mindedly
praise and make offerings exclusively — this is called right practice.]

Now, practice is of two kinds: first, right practice; second, mixed practice. Right practice is practice done exclusively in accordance with the rebirth sūtras — this is right practice. Which are the right practices? Single-mindedly and attentively reciting and reading the Contemplation Sūtra, the Amitābha Sūtra, the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, and so on; single-mindedly and attentively contemplating, observing, and recollecting the adornments of the
proper and dependent

rewards of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. If one bows to the Buddha, one bows single-mindedly and attentively to Amitābha Buddha; if one recites with the mouth, one recites single-mindedly and attentively the name of Amitābha Buddha; if one praises and makes offerings, one praises and makes offerings single-mindedly and attentively — only this is called right practice.

[Rebirth sūtras] The three Pure Land sūtras: the Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, the Contemplation Sūtra of Immeasurable Life, and the Amitābha Sūtra. [“Right practice”] Here the word “yan” is an initial particle without meaning. For example, “yan guiyu hao” simply means “to return to good terms.” [Two kinds of reward] The proper reward and the dependent reward. The proper reward is the body, because the body is what the karmic causes ripen into — it is the direct receiving of the reward, hence “proper reward.” The dependent reward is the resultant environment in which the body dwells, such as the land, houses, utensils, and so on.
[Moreover, within this right practice there are again two kinds: first,
single-mindedly
reciting exclusively
the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long,
never abandoning it thought after thought
(the thought of reciting the Buddha continuing without interruption, not replaced by deluded thoughts)
is called the karma of right concentration

, because it accords with that Buddha’s vow. If one practices in dependence on bowing, reciting, and so on, it is called supporting karma. Apart from these two kinds of practice, right and supporting, all other good deeds are called mixed practice. If one cultivates the above two kinds of practice, right and supporting, the mind constantly draws near [the Buddha], recollecting without interruption — this is called non-interruption.]

Moreover, within this right practice there are again two kinds: first, single-mindedly and attentively reciting exclusively the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of the length of time, never abandoning it thought after thought — this is called the karma of right concentration, because it accords with Amitābha Buddha’s fundamental vow. As for bowing to the Buddha, praising, making offerings, and so on, these are called supporting karma. Apart from these two kinds of practice, right and supporting, all other good deeds are called mixed practice. If one cultivates these two kinds of practice, right and supporting, the mind constantly draws near Amitābha Buddha, recollecting without interruption — this is non-interruption (no deluded thoughts mixed in)!

[Never abandoning it thought after thought] The thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption, not replaced by deluded thoughts. [Right concentration] Correct meditative absorption. When body and mind are pure and not scattered, it is called “right concentration.” [Karma] The activity of body, speech, and mind.
Question: Master Shandao’s Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles says:
Single-mindedly and exclusively recite
the name of Amitābha Buddha, and you will surely attain rebirth, without any doubt.”

The Primal Vow school interprets this passage as: “As long as one recites from a whole life’s recitation down to a single recitation or ten recitations, relying on Amitābha Buddha’s vow-power, one will surely be reborn.” So their conclusion is: Master Shandao taught that name-recitation ensures rebirth. But what, after all,
is single-minded exclusive recitation?
Answer:
Single-minded exclusive recitation is exclusively reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha without any distracting thoughts.
In the Treatise on Rebirth, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu says:
World-Honored One, I
single-mindedly
take refuge in the Tathāgata of Unobstructed Light pervading the ten directions, wishing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss.”
On this, Master Tanluan comments in his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth:
‘I
single-mindedly’
is Bodhisattva Vasubandhu’s word of self-admonition. It means that in recollecting the Tathāgata of Unobstructed Light and wishing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss,
thought follows thought in succession, with no other thoughts intermingled
Therefore, “
single-minded
means thought following thought in succession, with no other thoughts intermingled.
[Tathāgata of Unobstructed Light] One of the twelve epithets of Amitābha Buddha.
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu further says in the Treatise on Rebirth:
“The mind constantly makes vows,
single-mindedly and exclusively reciting
, in the end to be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss, wishing
truly to practice śamatha
This proves that “single-minded exclusive recitation” is exclusively reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha without any distracting thoughts.
[Śamatha] Translated as “calming.” To calm is
to still all distracting thoughts.
Therefore Master Shandao taught:
“An uninterrupted succession brings rebirth
(at the moment of death, if only the thought of reciting the Buddha continues without interruption by deluded thoughts, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
. If one can continue recitation thought after thought until the end of life
(one who practices thus all one’s life)
, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
Please note that what Master Shandao taught is
“an uninterrupted succession brings rebirth”
— single-minded exclusive recitation at the moment of death brings rebirth. It is not that name-recitation ensures rebirth!
Single-minded exclusive recitation
is supremely excellent. In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra in Four Fascicles, Master Shandao taught that single-minded exclusive recitation is the
“karma of right concentration.”
Master Shandao said:
Single-mindedly and exclusively recite
the name of Amitābha Buddha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of how long, never abandoning it thought after thought
(the thought of reciting the Buddha continuing without interruption, not replaced by deluded thoughts)
, this is called the
karma of right concentration
[Right concentration] Correct meditative absorption. When body and mind are pure and not scattered, it is called “right concentration.” [Karma] The activity of body, speech, and mind.
As to how one can be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, for details see
The Conditions for Rebirth
and
